review_notes: I read the whole file and checked how its lemmas are used in the library and tests. The existing simp lemmas (`primeSupportedIndices_empty`, `mem_primeSupportedIndices_univ`, `not_mem_primeSupportedIndices_zero`) look fine: each rewrites to a simpler form and they don't conflict. I found one missing simp lemma. I did not run Lean, so I don't know whether the suggested attribute interacts badly with other simp lemmas, such as the `Set.mem_setOf_eq` unfolding of set-builder supports. I deliberately did not suggest `@[simp]` for `mem_primeSupportedIndices_iff` or `mem_primeSupportedIndices_iff_factoredNumbers`. The first would unfold a membership predicate everywhere. The second only matches the narrow set `{p | p.1 ∈ s}`.

findings.excerpt:
theorem prime_mem_primeSupportedIndices_iff {S : Set Nat.Primes} (p : Nat.Primes) :
    p.1 ∈ primeSupportedIndices S ↔ p ∈ S := by
findings.problem: This lemma is the canonical normal form for membership of a coerced prime in `primeSupportedIndices S`. It rewrites to a strictly simpler goal (`p ∈ S`) and the left side is a clean pattern, `↑p ∈ primeSupportedIndices S`. It is not tagged `@[simp]`, although the file does tag the neighbouring membership facts `mem_primeSupportedIndices_univ` and `not_mem_primeSupportedIndices_zero`. Simp therefore cannot discharge or normalise such goals, and every caller applies `.mpr`/`.mp` by hand. Examples are `PrimeSupportedCoefficients.lean` lines 80 and 229, `IntegerPadicResidueLimit.lean` line 47, and the tests `two_supported_four` and `PrimeSupportedCoefficients` examples. The sibling `mem_primeSupportedIndices_iff` is deliberately non-simp, since it would unfold a membership predicate. This one is different: it replaces the predicate by an assumption-free, smaller statement.
findings.proposed_change: Mark it `@[simp] theorem prime_mem_primeSupportedIndices_iff ...`. Callers such as `(Nat.prime_mem_primeSupportedIndices_iff p).mpr hp` could then become `by simpa using hp`, or plain `simp [hp]` when the hypothesis is in context. The lemma is terminating and cycle-free. It has no side conditions, and no other simp lemma has the same left-hand side. Numeric literals like `2 ∈ primeSupportedIndices {twoPrime}` still need the `twoPrime` unfolding, so the benefit is for goals stated with a coerced `Nat.Primes` term. Optionally also add a `Set.mem_singleton_iff`-style test, since `p ∈ {q}` then reduces by existing simp lemmas.
findings.benefit: Simp becomes able to normalise membership of coerced primes in prime-supported submonoids. That removes the manual `.mpr`/`.mp` applications in downstream proofs and tests, and gives one canonical form for `↑p ∈ primeSupportedIndices S`.
